CLIPPER SHIP "CHALLENGE"
The front cover of this menu is a reproduction of an authentic Currier & Ives clipper ship print.
Currier & Ives, known as the "Printmakers of America", graphically preserved the glorious clipper
ship era in a magnificent series of clipper ship prints. This print, one of a series, is being reproduced
through the courtesy of The Mariners Museum, Newport News, Virginia.
William H. Webb launched the clipper ship "Challenge" in May, 1851, in New York City. She
was extreme in every way. Her spars were long, her spread of canvas enormous and her V-bottom
the sharpest of any clipper afloat. Her reputation too was extreme. Robert Waterman, Captain
of the "Challenge" had an infamous background which added to the difficulty of gathering a crew
for the hazardous trip around Cape Horn. With a crew of sixty-four men it took the "Challenge"
109 days to reach California. Mutiny had broken out and drastic measures were used to enforce
obedience. Newspapers in San Francisco erupted into a series of virulent accusations by the crew
against the Captain. Although he was later exonerated, the name of "Challenge" had been dis-
credited. In 1859 she made her last passage under the American flag. The principal error in her
design was her hollow waterline which sapped her power and slowed her passage through the water.
